items.title: Jim Crow returns…one congressional district at a time.
items.author: bounce-mc.us1_388705.10708631-d186966748@mail66.atl71.mcdlv.net
items.content:
One of the defining issues heading into this year’s midterms is how redistricting has rapidly reshaped electoral maps across the country. When the Supreme Court gutted much of the Voting Rights Act earlier this year, a number of states redrew maps eliminating majority-Black districts, weakening Black political power potentially for years to come.

But what does this shift feel like for someone working on the ground to expand voting access for Black communities when the promise of equal representation itself is under assault? Ask LaTosha Brown, co-founder of Black Voters Matter Fund, a group that’s been working to increase voter participation within minority communities in the rural South, especially where turnout is low.

“There are people who are openly white supremacists that are consolidating power at record speed in such a way that they are stripping away all of the rights, opportunities, and access points for you and your family,” she says, referring to communities of color in the South. “If that don’t move you, it ain’t nothing that I can say that can move you.”

, Brown talks with host Al Letson about her winding path into politics, her fight against ongoing voter suppression efforts in the South, and why it’s important to mobilize Black voters now more than ever.

items.title: We're tracking 76 ongoing anti-voting lawsuits (and counting)
items.author: 1axbn3qnmubd8o3t6lh6ovkj3rby1u13akv9gj@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
To say there’s a lot going on with voting in North Carolina would be an understatement. A state board of elections meeting could yield anything from voter suppression by Chick-fil-A’s weekend hours to voter suppression led by partisan operatives to voter suppression manifesting in threats to arrest student meeting attendees.

Notice a trend? You aren’t alone. So did the nearly a dozen voters, experts and election officials I spoke to marking the start of early voting in the Tar Heel state.

In short, hurdles to voting access are not one-off instances. For marginalized communities, they’re embedded in the very fabric of the state. This fall, the GOP-controlled elections board for students and majority-Black neighborhoods, slashed Sunday voting hours in half, a slew of confusing letters asking for various levels of voter identification information, and made it easier to reject mail ballots.

Mail ballot restrictions are facing fierce , and we’re awaiting a ruling any day now that would either block or uphold a rule that voters must seal an inner envelope tucked, as one voter described to me, “like an eighth of an inch” away from the outer envelope.

It’s a nearly impossible task for those with tremors or other mobility constraints. But it’s already spoiling ballots, according to multiple county election officials who spoke to me for this story. And we didn’t even get to the fact that North Carolina is a major battleground in this election.

The stakes truly couldn’t be higher.

items.title: When trees fall in a golf course, do they make a sound?
items.author: bounce_4e2016e8-e7c8-f111-bf5b-000d3a4fbe83_prod@bounce.myngp.com
items.content:
Thanks to committed plaintiffs, good lawyers, and a federal judge carefully applying the law, the destruction of hundreds of trees at a public golf course is now being heard across the country. 

Earlier this year, the DC Preservation League and two frequent golfers at East Potomac Golf Course sued the Department of the Interior and the National Park Service, challenging plans by the President to transform the existing historic public golf course into “an elite champion-style course.” 

Through multiple court hearings, the judge initially declined to enter injunctive relief. Instead, she directed the government to provide advance notice of substantive construction work and accepted the government’s assurances that it would do so. 

However, in the early morning of Saturday, October 10, as noted in a subsequent order by the court, the government “…razed nearly 430 trees, none of which were hazardous or posed safety concerns.”

With each thud of the 430 trees needlessly destroyed during that holiday weekend, there was a corresponding blow to the justice system. A judge had expected that the government would act in good faith and in accordance with commitments made in a court of law. Instead, that government rushed to bypass those assurances in order to reshape a public resource in line with the President’s vision, with many questions unanswered, including about future public access and affordability.

On October 13, the judge issued that temporary restraining order. For the government, it was another severe blow to the presumption of trust and honest dealing that Department of Justice lawyers previously had brought with them into the courtroom. As the judge stated in her opinion: 

“Breakneck speed to clear trees that posed no harm.  The reason?  Disputed.  The budget?  Unclear. The environmental impact?  Unstudied. The urgency?  None.  Next steps:  bulldoze hundreds more.”

This is not simply a case about whether trees were removed in noncompliance with regulatory programs that would apply to a massive overhaul of a public space. Rather, this is an example of what happens when respect for the rule of law erodes. This case demonstrates how difficult it is for the courts to keep up with an administration that ignores rules that apply to everyone else, spurns judicial directives, and then sends government lawyers to appear before judges, caught between trying to please their employer and possibly risking their own license to practice law in doing so.

Joyce Vance, Distinguished Professor of the Practice of Law at the University of Alabama School of Law and a former United States Attorney, has written about the importance of holding on to the moral compass that allows us to distinguish right from wrong. Recognizing how exhausting it is to watch “attacks on democracy unfold every day,” she urges that we “never be quiet about it”. 

Indeed, that is a responsibility we all share. Speak out. Protect the rule of law. Defend judges who apply the law, even as they risk attacks from their own government.

When trees fall, be the sound that is heard everywhere.

Lawyers Defending American Democracy

P.S. Thank you for your ongoing support of LDAD. Please help us protect the rule of law and the freedoms we hold dear by volunteering for our Meeting the Moment initiative and donating to our work.

items.title: The law might finally be catching up to DOGE
items.author: delivery_20261015091552.47947129.281@bounce.slate.com
items.content:
Believe it or not, it’s been over a year since Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency tore through the U.S. government, infamously shuttering the U.S. Agency for International Development while falsely claiming it had saved America $52.8 billion. Throughout its 10-month run, DOGE was dodging a Freedom of Information Act request from a public interest group, which eventually led to a lawsuit that sought to force the agency to hand over internal records that would reveal how it was making decisions. The dispute has been simmering for over a year now, ping-ponging between lower courts, appeals court panels, and the Supreme Court as the Trump administration has been pushing to protect DOGE from any public disclosures. But now, this fight might finally be coming to an end, as the Supreme Court agreed this week to consider the case, for a second time—the first time, SCOTUS sided with the Trump administration by forcing a lower court to reevaluate its order forcing it to hand over DOGE’s records—and Its decision stands to impact what responsibility all federal agencies have to the public—if any.

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court agreed to hear arguments in U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, where the justices will weigh in on whether DOGE should be classified as a federal agency, and therefore subject to FOIA requests—a federal mandate that gives any person the right to access records from federal executive branch agencies. The Trump administration has been insisting for the past year that DOGE was not a federal agency, but a presidential advisory body, and therefore not subject to FOIA. However, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, the watchdog group suing, is calling foul, noting that DOGE was given taxpayer dollars to the tune of $41 million to fund its operations. DOGE also incorrectly sought to apply the standard—a 2004 case that shielded the executive branch from complying with public records requests—in order to maintain autonomy of its office and safeguard confidentiality of its communications, the lawsuit argues.

This case will be critical in holding DOGE accountable for not just the utter destruction it caused within the U.S. government, but in setting a clear precedent for how U.S. presidents can or cannot bypass federal disclosure laws. For decades, journalists in particular have relied on FOIA to unearth waste, abuse, and ethics violations committed by the U.S. government, something that’s become alarmingly common under Trump.

CREW first filed FOIA requests with DOGE in January 2025, around the time President Donald Trump established the agency via executive order. The watchdog group noted that Musk was tasked with running DOGE even though he never received official congressional approval and was operating “seemingly unchecked, with no clarity on its structure, staffing, budget or operations, including whether it is following federal ethics and transparency laws or even acting within its legal authority,” CREW said in a statement. The group’s goal was to arm Congress with critical information that could inform its upcoming appropriations cycle. However, things did not go to plan.

The Trump administration flatly refused to comply with CREW’s records request, while DOGE fired tens of thousands of federal employees, collected Americans’ most sensitive data, and dismantled core agencies like USAID, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Department of Education, and more. By February 2025, CREW had filed a lawsuit in order to force DOGE’s cooperation. In court the Trump administration argued DOGE was not legally required to comply with FOIA requests because it was not technically a federal agency. U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper disagreed with that assessment and concluded that DOGE was likely subject to FOIA “because it is endowed with and is apparently exercising ‘substantial authority independent of the President.’ ”

Unsatisfied, the Trump administration tried to appeal Cooper’s order but was rejected by the D.C. appeals court panel. Come May 2025, the administration decided to knock on the Supreme Court’s door, asking the justices to stay Cooper’s order, and they agreed. In an unsigned order, they said Cooper’s order was overly broad and needed to “counsel judicial deference and restraint in the context of discovery regarding internal Executive Branch communications.” In response, CREW amended its FOIA request to exclude any information about recommendations DOGE staffers made directly to the White House. Lower courts declined to block its records request, effectively forcing the Trump administration to hand over the bulk of CREW’s original FOIA request.

Still dissatisfied with having to give even an inch, the Trump administration did not comply with that ruling, and instead came back to SCOTUS this year, asking the justices to consider the case on its merits and assess all of CREW’s FOIA requests of federal agencies, from DOGE and beyond. It accused Cooper of continuing to approve “intrusive discovery against a presidential advisory body without adequate consideration for the separation of powers, the FOIA statute,” and the Supreme Court’s order from last year. The administration wants SCOTUS to apply the standard, while CREW has argued “this case looks nothing like ,” and if it did it would effectively foreclose discovery in this case, which is not what SCOTUS said in last year’s order.

items.title: I owe you a thank you
items.author: 1axb2levevzi9w9n1roire2udyx7yq6d2p43oj@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
It is true that the future of free and fair elections is playing out in courthouses across the country. But it is not enough for lawyers to litigate. They have an obligation to speak publicly and plainly about these cases.

This is not a new frustration for me. For years, I have watched Republican lawyers take center stage promoting election-denial conspiracy theories while those charged with defending democracy hide behind their legal filings.

During the Biden presidency, this disagreement spilled into public view when some in the White House criticized me for “fighting on every possible front — filing a flurry of lawsuits and exerting public pressure through the media.”

Since Trump’s return to power, those critics have largely gone quiet. Yet too few people are willing to take on Trump directly, without caveats or false equivalence.

Meanwhile, I have redoubled my efforts. I have continued to litigate, arguing in federal and state courts, including before the U.S. Supreme Court last term.

My law firm is currently litigating nearly 90 voting and election cases in 41 states. They include some of the most consequential cases for the future of democracy and free and fair elections. The firm is also preparing for what may come next: post-election litigation, recounts and election contests.

Even so, I refuse to stop speaking out. I won’t simply let my legal filings do the talking.

That is why I write for Democracy Docket several times a week. It is why I travel and give speeches. It is why I have expanded my video essays on YouTube.

I make time to share my opinions on the state of voting and democracy, along with my analysis of what is happening in court, because educating the public is as important as arguing before judges.

Usually, that means writing late at night or on weekends. It means recording podcasts at odd hours.

Those hours add up, and earlier this week, I admitted to you that I was tired.

So many of you wrote back to tell me you were rooting for me, to ask how I was holding up and to remind me to take care of myself. Some of you said you were tired, too. I read those messages, and they meant more to me than I can say. Thank you.

Over the past six years, Democracy Docket has grown beyond my wildest expectations. It now includes daily and weekly newsletters, opinion pieces, breaking news, investigative journalism, a podcast and more.

With more than 500,000 free newsletter subscribers and millions of monthly visitors to our website, our reach and influence continue to expand. That is all good news.

But here is the thing: Democracy Docket is reader-funded. There are no corporate owners or outside investors. We rely on people like you to grow.

If now is not the right time for you to become a premium member, I offer my warmest thanks for staying informed and remaining part of this community.

If, however, you simply haven’t gotten around to upgrading, or aren’t sure whether to do so, I ask you to consider what Democracy Docket means to you and to the pro-democracy movement. With the midterms less than 30 days away, our mission is more urgent than ever.

Democracy will not protect itself from Trump’s lies. It requires people willing to stand up and speak out — loudly, persistently and in plain language. That is what I try to do. It is what the Democracy Docket team does. I hope you will stand with us.

items.title: 64 cases, zero proof: Putting Bannon’s lie to bed
items.author: 1axceynr3fctrz2of4p6mg8658sin53im00kbn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
This weekend, in an interview with Ted Koppel on CBS’s , Steve Bannon confirmed what I have been saying for years: “The core belief of the MAGA movement is [Trump] won the 2020 election.”

When confronted with the fact that Trump and his allies lost more than 60 court cases challenging the election results, Bannon resorted to a familiar GOP tactic. He falsely suggested that the cases were thrown out on technicalities: “We can go debate this another time, but we didn’t have standing. We never even got into court.”

Even worse, Koppel told viewers that Bannon was “technically correct; they didn’t have standing. They couldn’t find a judge who thought they had a significant case worth hearing.”

Koppel may have meant that the cases failed because they lacked merit. But what he said is simply wrong.

Trump and his allies found plenty of judges willing to hear them out, in many cases through hours or even days of testimony and argument. Those judges listened, weighed the evidence and ruled against them.

I know, because I was the lawyer who helped Joe Biden defeat those cases one by one.

Correcting the record matters as we approach another election in which Trump and the GOP are once again spreading lies. So let me put this one to bed, once and for all.

items.title: Trump hates me personally. Now he’s taking it to the Supreme Court.
items.author: 1axclmoswx0laweygwujfiy434hzby2f7wrfmr@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
When I tell people that Donald Trump hates me, they often assume I mean it in a generic sense — that he hates Democrats and people who fight him in court. No, I correct them: he hates me personally.

On Friday, he took that hatred to the U.S. Supreme Court.

In 2022, Trump sued me, along with Hillary Clinton and several others, for racketeering. A federal judge dismissed the case and sanctioned Trump and his lawyers, ultimately ordering Trump and his lead attorney to pay nearly $1 million.

On appeal, a unanimous panel of the conservative 11th Circuit, including a judge appointed by Trump, upheld both the dismissal and the sanctions.

Now Trump wants the Supreme Court to revive his suit and throw out the sanctions.

His lawyers argue that he deserves extra time to sue because he set the case aside while serving as president. They also claim the Court must step in to protect the presidency from judges who punish its lawyers.

Trump filed this suit as a private citizen, between his two terms. The 11th Circuit found his claims not only too late but “otherwise meritless,” and it agreed that many of the legal arguments he and his lawyer made were frivolous.

I became a defendant in this lawsuit because, in 2016, I represented Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign.

When Russia hacked the Democratic Party and the campaign, my role as general counsel required me to understand what happened. That required assessing Russia's interest in interfering in the campaign, weighing legal options and risks.

At a news conference in July 2016, Trump said: “Russia, if you’re listening, I hope you’re able to find the 30,000 emails that are missing. I think you will probably be rewarded mightily by our press.”

On that point, Trump was right.

The legacy media basked in every email leak. The fact that they were the product of a foreign government’s effort to swing the election did not matter to them or their corporate bosses.

“But her emails” became shorthand for that coverage, and the legacy media has never reckoned with it.

That failure, like its coverage of the Iraq War in 2003, is part of the reason Democrats’ confidence in the legacy media has eroded. I believe it is also why independent outlets like Democracy Docket have grown while the legacy media struggles.

Once he became president, Trump waged a multi-year war against me and others who worked for the Clinton campaign. During his first term, his supporters spread lies and misinformation. Ultimately, his Department of Justice appointed a special counsel to pursue us.

Anyone who thinks weaponization started in Trump’s second term has forgotten John Durham’s appointment and the partisan witch hunt that followed.

After three and a half years of nonstop investigation, Durham charged just three people. One was an FBI lawyer with no connection to the campaign. He pleaded guilty to altering an email and was sentenced to probation.

The other two were charged with lying to the FBI, went to trial and were quickly acquitted. One of them was a former law partner of mine.

Durham clearly hoped to dig up dirt on me, but in the end, he failed. I was never charged.

The experience left me with a keen understanding of how Trump can turn his army of supporters against someone while casting himself as the victim.

items.title: Al Letson challenged a conservative activist on voter fraud. He abruptly ended the interview.
items.author: bounce-mc.us1_388705.10708550-d186966748@mail194.suw241.rsgsv.net
items.content:
Readers, this week, you’re in for two firsts: the show’s first full-length video episode and its first guest to angrily storm off mid-interview. 

While interviewing conservative activist J. Christian Adams, host Al Letson challenged his claims of widespread voter fraud in the US—a claim that’s been widely debunked. After 13 minutes of back and forth, Adams abruptly left the interview, a moment that you can see right

here on our Instagram page.

Don’t worry, this week’s episode isn’t 14 minutes long.

national voting rights correspondent Ari Berman swooped in at the eleventh hour. We even got Berman’s take on Adams’ quick departure:

“If he feels so confident in his numbers and arguments, why would he be so defensive from the very beginning to extremely basic and fair questions that you were asking? You weren’t asking him gotcha questions. You were asking him very basic questions to defend his assertions, and he immediately got so defensive. It reminded me of President Donald Trump storming off

when Kristen Welker pushed him on the 2020 election."

But this episode is so much more than Adams. In it, Letson and Berman take a serious look at Adams’ and the Trump administration’s claims of voter fraud, their lack of evidence, and how they’re using these claims to rig the upcoming midterm elections. Trust me, it’s an episode you won’t want to miss.

items.title: I won’t let my legal briefs do the talking
items.author: 1axbipo1irgzb0g5p0jb9p2t006x8r6vwo6ztv@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Now is not the time to hide. It is the time to stand tall and speak out.

That is the message I have delivered at a series of events over the past few weeks. I have spoken to diverse audiences of business leaders, lawyers, students and concerned citizens.

At each event, I was warmly received. People praised my work as a lawyer and as a vocal opponent of Donald Trump’s efforts to subvert democracy.

Yet when I called on the audience to act and speak out, I too often heard the usual concerns: “I am just one person.” “My friends are MAGA.” “My clients or customers won’t like it.”

I recently sat down with Semafor for an interview about Democracy Docket. The host noted that most lawyers prefer to let their legal briefs do the talking. Why, he wanted to know, don’t I follow that same approach?

My answer was the same one I gave my audience: it is too dangerous to stay silent.

It is true that the future of free and fair elections is playing out in courthouses across the country. But it is not enough for lawyers to litigate. They have an obligation to speak publicly and plainly about these cases.

This is not a new frustration for me. For years, I have watched Republican lawyers take center stage promoting election-denial conspiracy theories while those charged with defending democracy hide behind their legal filings.

During the Biden presidency, this disagreement spilled into public view when some in the White House criticized me for “fighting on every possible front — filing a flurry of lawsuits and exerting public pressure through the media.”

Since Trump’s return to power, those critics have largely gone quiet. Yet too few people are willing to take on Trump directly, without caveats or false equivalence.

Meanwhile, I have redoubled my efforts. I have continued to litigate, arguing in federal and state courts, including before the U.S. Supreme Court last term.

My law firm is currently litigating nearly 90 voting and election cases in 41 states. They include some of the most consequential cases for the future of democracy and free and fair elections. The firm is also preparing for what may come next: post-election litigation, recounts and election contests.

Even so, I refuse to stop speaking out. I won’t simply let my legal filings do the talking.

items.title: Who will stop Trump now from seizing voting machines?
items.author: 1axb2a54qx7g67d6wvvnght97tmq66zafeh1ur@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Convicted criminal and former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters is pushing a scheme to give the Trump administration control over voting machines. In August, she called on the Department of War “to go in and demand to have these machines in their custody.”

More recently, her lawyer, election denier Peter Ticktin, suggested that Peters’ plan was to “get control over the ballots as soon as the machine spits them through and then do a recount.” And on Oct. 5, according to Trump ally Ed Martin, Peters met with Trump in the Oval Office to discuss election security.

We have been here before.

In December 2020, a group of conspiracy theorists sat in the Oval Office arguing that Donald Trump should declare a national emergency and order the secretary of defense to “seize, collect, retain and analyze” voting machines, equipment and electronically stored election information.

The motley crew of election deniers pushing this approach included attorney Sidney Powell, Trump’s former national security adviser Michael Flynn and former Overstock.com CEO Patrick Byrne. The day before the meeting, Flynn had suggested that the president could invoke martial law and use the military to “rerun” elections in swing states.

More important than who advocated seizing voting equipment was who opposed it. The White House counsel, his deputy and the staff secretary all helped stop Trump from signing the order. So did Attorney General William Barr. Even Rudy Giuliani opposed using the military.

Those guardrails no longer exist.

items.title: Action Alert: Speak Out Against Taxpayer-Funded Political Ads
items.author: bounce_75b4552d-49c3-f111-bf5b-000d3a4fbe83_prod@bounce.myngp.com
items.content:
This administration’s “flood the zone” strategy continues with actions that raise serious concerns about constitutional principles and the rule of law. As disheartening as these actions can be, we must meet them with informed engagement and expectations for a better future.

Today, we are issuing our latest Action Alert, asking the public to speak out against the misuse of federal resources for partisan political promotion. 

The administration recently spent nearly $12 million in taxpayer funds on television ads promoting the President, with millions more allocated under a $20 million contract for additional ads selected to run during major broadcasts in the critical weeks before the midterm elections. Following widespread criticism, the President announced that the remaining ads would be paid for via his MAGA Inc. Super PAC.

Both approaches raise serious questions under federal law, including restrictions on the use of appropriated funds for unauthorized publicity or political propaganda, the Hatch Act, and federal campaign finance laws. Shifting the payment method from taxpayer funding to privately raised Super PAC funds does not eliminate the need to comply with applicable legal restrictions. 

Our Action Alert outlines four steps you can take today.

LDAD is grateful to our many volunteers who continue to help document important developments, raise concerns, and defend the rule of law. They do this in a variety of ways, for example:

LDAD volunteer, Professor Mark Gordon, recently moderated an important election-related program co-sponsored by the Minnesota State Bar Association and LDAD entitled: Rules and Procedures for Voting in the Midterm Elections in MN.

Lawyers Defending American Democracy

P.S. Thank you for your ongoing support of LDAD. Please help us protect the rule of law and the freedoms we hold dear by volunteering for our Meeting the Moment initiative and donating to our work.

items.title: Trump is doing family separation but without the backlash
items.author: delivery_20261008060502.47827077.141@bounce.slate.com
items.content:
Children are almost always treated with special deference in American law, because lawmakers understand and respect the significance of adolescence and the necessity of parental guidance. President Donald Trump has upended this long-standing, universal understanding in a particularly insidious way during his second term. For the first time in our nation’s history, tens of thousands of children are being separated from their parents, who, at the hands of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, are being violently arrested inside of the country, then detained, and quickly deported without their kids. These children are essentially left to fend for themselves or are placed with an unknown caregiver, which in some cases has led to horrific endings. Although this may sound awfully similar to Trump’s 2018 “zero-tolerance” policy, it is worse, because there is no explicit family separation policy this time around, making it harder to challenge in court. Instead, family separation has become just another devastating consequence of the president’s mass deportation agenda.

Under past administrations, ICE policy held that any detainees who were parents should be reunited with their children before being deported, or agents must get confirmation that there is a designated caregiver in place for their children in the parents’ absence. Last year, upon Trump returning to the White House, ICE revised this policy to make it only applicable “when operationally feasible,” which gave agents all the leeway they needed to ignore the historical guidance in order to prioritize mass deportations. “This loosening of guidelines, combined with scaled-up immigration enforcement, has resulted in the detention of thousands of parents, many of whose minor children are U.S. citizens,” a recent analysis by the Migration Policy Institute concluded.

Under Trump 2.0, the Department of Homeland Security no longer provides reliable data on its immigration enforcement, but the Brookings Institution estimates that as of April 2026 about 205,000 children have likely experienced a parental detention since Trump began his second term and about 145,000 of these children are U.S. citizens. Mothers in particular seem to be affected, with ProPublica finding that the Trump administration is deporting about four times as many moms of U.S. citizen children per day as the Biden administration did, most of whom have minor or no criminal histories at all. 

Stories of these children are playing out across the country, like in Minnesota, where three children have been separated from their father for nearly 10 months after he was yanked out of his car and violently arrested on his way to work. And in Alabama, where one woman has been caring for an old co-worker’s 2-year-old for nearly a year since ICE picked up the baby’s mother while she was on a grocery run. In Illinois, a college senior found himself the sole breadwinner of his family after ICE arrested and detained his uncle. Three sisters in San Francisco were among a lucky few who were reunited with their mother after she was detained for almost a year, leaving the eldest sibling to take care of the household while juggling college classes and navigating a complicated immigration system for her mother.

Then there are the children who ICE arrests with one or both of their parents. Although the U.S. government has historically allowed families to remain in detention together, the Trump administration has quietly been separating children by giving their parents false promises that they’ll be able to stay in touch with them. In reality, as detailed by Mother Jones, oftentimes children are sent to the Office of Refugee Resettlement and reclassified as unaccompanied minors—they are not; the U.S. government knows their parents are in detention—and sent off to live with foster parents. ORR does not track these types of cases, so it's unclear how many children are being reclassified, but Mother Jones estimated they now make up a “huge chunk” of ORR’s caseload. Under normal circumstances, unaccompanied minors are defined as children who arrive at a U.S. border alone, with no parent or guardian. 

Regardless of how the Trump administration chooses to manipulate immigration law, the National Immigration Law Center says parents and legal guardians who are detained by ICE have a legal right to make decisions about their minor child’s care. They are also allowed to see their children while in detention, upon written request, whether that’s in person or over a video or phone call. And if a parent faces deportation, they also have a legal right to make decisions about what happens to their children, which usually comes down to either allowing the child to remain in the U.S., regardless of the child’s immigration status, or to be deported alongside the parent. All of these decisions are supposed to happen with a lawyer, but even this is no longer happening, due to financial constraints, the administration’s attacks on legal aid for minors, and its extreme hostility toward immigrants, leaving parents with little to no recourse when ICE does not follow protocol. 

Children do not get to choose their parents’ immigration status, yet their families are being torn apart over it. The consequences are clear, with studies showing that children who lose a parent to sudden, forced deportation experience anxiety, anger, aggression, isolation, and depression. It also often leads to housing instability, academic withdrawal, and family dissolution. Yet, the president is unbothered by this; in fact, he’s doubled down on efforts to eliminate immigrant children from the U.S. altogether, evidenced by his birthright citizenship executive order. Despite the Supreme Court categorically rejecting it earlier this year, Trump has since introduced yet another executive order targeting birthright citizenship.

The Trump administration’s assault on immigrants has been cruel at every turn, but what it’s doing to immigrant children could be its worst act by far.

items.title: I told you I was tired. Then I read about ICE.
items.author: 1axbgqdukd9tcdf9saw0c5kozh3g0t0g1nbwe7@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
By last spring, ICE was already laying the groundwork to interfere in the midterms. Explosive new documents show that it had investigated groups that register voters, considered infiltrating some of them with undercover agents, and amassed tens of millions of voter records.

For months, I have been sounding the alarm that ICE will be used to suppress voters and block people from casting their ballots. These records show that, behind the scenes, it is already carrying out Trump's orders.

None of this is an accident. When President Donald Trump returned to office, he set out to build an army ahead of the midterms — one that would answer to him and only him.
